name: application-danger-zone-panel
title: Danger Zone Panel
description: A visually separated, red-bordered settings section grouping destructive account or project actions, each guarded by a confirmation step.
useWhen: A settings page has one or more irreversible actions (delete account, delete project, leave organization) that should be visually set apart from routine settings.
Each destructive action needs a description of its consequences alongside the trigger, not just a bare button.
avoidWhen: The action is reversible or low-stakes — mixing it into this panel overstates its severity and trains users to ignore the warning styling.
You only have a single destructive action with no other settings context — a standalone alert dialog trigger may be simpler than a full panel.
responsiveBehavior: Each row is a flex layout that keeps the label and description on the left and the action button pinned right; on narrow viewports, wrap the row to stack the button below the text if the button label is long.
accessibility: The panel is a <section> with aria-labelledby pointing at the "Danger zone" heading, so screen readers announce it as a distinct region.
Every destructive trigger opens a confirmation dialog (see the alert-dialog component) rather than acting immediately — irreversible actions should never fire on a single accidental click.
Color (red border/text) is reinforced by explicit heading and description text, never relying on color alone to convey severity.

variants.title: Single action
variants.description: One destructive row (delete account) wired to an alert dialog confirmation
accessibility: The trigger button opens a dialog rather than deleting immediately, giving the user a chance to back out.

variants.description: One destructive row (delete account) wired to an alert dialog confirmation

variants.title: Multiple actions
variants.description: Three destructive rows (transfer ownership, leave organization, delete project) grouped in one panel with a shared header
accessibility: Each row's button carries its own accessible name via visible text, distinguishing otherwise similarly styled destructive actions.
